questions.question: What is the core mechanism of EAGLE-3 speculative decoding?
options: A smaller model generates a complete response, which the target model scores and either accepts or rewrites
Draft heads trained on the target model's hidden states propose k candidate tokens; the target model verifies all k in a single forward pass
The target model generates N responses in parallel and selects the highest-probability one
A lookup cache maps common prompt prefixes to precomputed continuations
questions.explanation: EAGLE-3 trains draft heads on the target model's hidden states. These heads propose k tokens per step. The target model verifies all k in one pass; accepted prefixes advance, rejected suffixes are resampled. This is the source of the 2.5-3x throughput gain.

questions.question: Why does tail latency (p99) worsen under rejection in speculative decoding?
options: The target model must reload its weights after each rejected batch of draft tokens
When the draft is rejected, the verify pass still ran (cost paid) but produced no net throughput gain, so that request takes a full verify-pass overhead with no acceleration
Rejected batches trigger a fallback to ngram drafting, which has higher per-token latency
The HPA scales down replicas during high rejection phases, reducing available capacity
questions.explanation: On a rejection, the verify pass consumed time and compute but yielded fewer accepted tokens than expected. High-rejection requests see worse tail latency than non-speculative decoding because the overhead of the verify pass is paid without the throughput benefit.

questions.question: What is the acceptance rate and what distribution-related risk does it face in production?
options: The fraction of input tokens that pass the content-safety filter before reaching the model

The fraction of drafted tokens the target model accepts; it drifts downward when the traffic distribution (e.g., domain data vs ShareGPT) diverges from the distribution the draft heads were trained on
The fraction of SWE-bench tasks where the agent's first proposed fix compiles without errors
The fraction of K8s HPA scale-out events that successfully reduce queue-wait below the target
questions.explanation: Acceptance rate is the fraction of drafted tokens accepted by the target. It is traffic-distribution-dependent: a draft trained on ShareGPT may have a 75% acceptance rate on general chat but drop significantly on domain-specific or code-heavy traffic.

questions.question: What metric does the Kubernetes HPA use to scale the inference server, and why is it better than CPU?
options: GPU memory utilization; GPU memory is the first resource exhausted during high load
Queue-wait time (time a request waits in the pending queue); this directly reflects user-visible latency, unlike CPU which may be low even when the GPU is the bottleneck
Tokens per second; a direct measure of throughput makes HPA decisions more accurate
Number of active WebSocket connections; each connection represents an active inference request
questions.explanation: Queue-wait time is the time a request spends waiting before inference starts, directly measuring latency impact on users. CPU utilization is often low on GPU servers even under full load, making it a poor HPA signal.

questions.question: What is P-EAGLE and how does it differ from serial EAGLE-3?
options: P-EAGLE uses a pretrained language model as the draft instead of trained heads
P-EAGLE runs parallel speculation over a tree of draft branches verified in one target pass, enabling deeper draft trees than serial EAGLE-3
P-EAGLE is a pruned version of EAGLE-3 that uses 50% fewer draft head parameters
P-EAGLE applies speculative decoding only to the prefill phase, not the decode phase
questions.explanation: P-EAGLE (from AWS 2026) extends EAGLE-3 with parallel speculation: instead of a single draft chain, it explores a tree of branches and verifies the entire tree in one target forward pass, enabling deeper speculation at higher acceptance rates on suitable traffic.

questions.question: What does the cost comparison report in this capstone measure, and what is its credibility purpose?
options: It compares GPTQ vs AWQ vs GGUF quantization cost at the same throughput level
It reports dollars per 1M output tokens for the self-hosted speculative-decoding setup vs Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.4, demonstrating the economic case for self-hosted inference
It measures the incremental cost of training EAGLE-3 draft heads vs using ngram fallback
It benchmarks K8s HPA scale-out costs against a fixed-replica deployment
questions.explanation: The cost comparison is the credibility lever: computing $/1M output tokens for your self-hosted vLLM + EAGLE-3 setup versus hosted Anthropic and OpenAI APIs on the same eval quantifies whether self-hosting is economically justified.
